title: HTML Forms and Accessibility Basics
description: Understand how browsers collect and submit form data, associate labels with controls, use native constraints, group related choices, and make forms operable with a keyboard and assistive technology.
learningOutcomes: Explain the roles of form, action, and method.
Associate a visible label with its control using for and id.
Distinguish id, name, placeholder, required, type, and autocomplete.
Choose appropriate controls and group related radio choices.
Build and keyboard-test an accessible registration form.

blocks.text: A form is a browser-native way to collect related values and submit them as a request. Its controls are not simply styled boxes: each has a role, state, constraints, and a way its value is represented during submission. A login form, search form, and address form may look different, but they share the same model: controls collect values, constraints can prevent invalid submission, and the form defines where and how a successful submission is sent.

blocks.title: Keep four questions separate
blocks.text: Which control collects the value? Which label explains that control? Which name identifies the value in submitted data? Which action receives the request? These are separate responsibilities. Confusing them often creates forms that look correct but are difficult to use or submit unexpected data.
The form and its submission contract

The example uses a hypothetical server route. It demonstrates HTML structure; it will not create an account unless a real server endpoint exists and implements the request. HTML defines the browser-side contract, not the backend behavior.

steps.title: form, action, and method
steps.explanation: The form groups controls into one submission. action names the destination URL and method defines how the request is sent. The /signup path is illustrative; a server must implement it before the form can create an account.

steps.title: label and for
steps.explanation: The label's for value matches the input's id. This explicit association makes the label clickable and gives the control an accessible name. The visible label remains available while the user types.

steps.title: id versus name
steps.explanation: id identifies the element in the document and participates in the label association. name identifies the value in submitted form data. A control can have an id and label but normally contributes no named value when it has no name.

steps.title: type, required, and autocomplete
steps.explanation: type=email gives the browser the intended input semantics and basic format validation. required prevents an empty value from passing native validation. autocomplete=email helps browsers and password managers recognize the field. These improvements do not replace server validation.

steps.title: password constraints
steps.explanation: type=password masks the visible characters; it does not encrypt the value. autocomplete=new-password signals a new credential field, while minlength adds a client-side constraint that must also be checked on the server.

steps.title: explicit submit button
steps.explanation: type=submit submits the form when native validation passes. Explicitly stating the type prevents ambiguity when additional buttons are later added.

blocks.text: GET places submitted values into the URL query string and is appropriate for repeatable requests without secrets, such as searches and filters. POST sends the form data in the request body and is commonly used when a request creates or changes server state. POST is not encryption: HTTPS protects data in transit, and server-side authorization and validation are still required. Never put passwords or other secrets in a GET URL.
How a control contributes submitted data

items: name is the key used for a control's value in submitted form data; id is a document identifier and is not a substitute for name.
Disabled controls are not submitted. Read-only controls behave differently and may still be included.
Unchecked checkboxes and radio buttons are not submitted as selected values.
A select submits the value of the selected option. Specify option value if the transmitted value should differ from its visible label.
A textarea's content is its value. Placeholder is only a hint and should not carry essential instructions.

blocks.text: A label communicates what a field is for. A common explicit pattern is label for="email" paired with input id="email". The values must match, and an id should be unique in the document. A label can also wrap a control implicitly, but use one clear pattern consistently. Placeholder may show an optional example, but it usually disappears while typing and is not a replacement for a visible label.

blocks.title: A placeholder is not a label
blocks.text: A field that only says “Email address” inside the control becomes unclear once the user starts typing. Keep a visible label, and use placeholder only for a supplementary example such as name@example.com.
Choose an input type for the data

items: text collects one line of free text.
email gives the browser a semantic hint and basic native validation for an email-like value.
password masks the displayed characters but does not encrypt the value.
number is for numeric quantities; a phone number is an identifier, not a quantity, so number is usually inappropriate for it.
checkbox is an independently selectable option.
radio represents one choice from options sharing the same name.
select chooses from a constrained list; textarea collects multiline text.

blocks.text: Group related controls with fieldset and legend

When several controls form one question—such as choosing a contact preference—group them with fieldset and describe the group with legend. Each control still needs its own id and label. Radio options in one group share a name so the browser treats them as mutually exclusive choices.

blocks.caption: An accessible radio group
blocks.code: Preferred contact method

items: button type="submit" submits the associated form.
button type="button" has no built-in submission behavior; it is for another interaction, often implemented with JavaScript.
button type="reset" restores controls to their initial values. Use it only when resetting is genuinely useful, because it can surprise users.
When a button is inside a form and its type is omitted, its default behavior is commonly submission. Set type explicitly to document intent.

blocks.text: Native validation and accessible error feedback

Attributes such as required, type=email, minlength, maxlength, min, max, and pattern let the browser check some constraints before submitting. The browser can focus an invalid control and expose a message. These checks can be bypassed, so the server must repeat important validation. In custom validation, explain the problem in text, associate a message with its field using aria-describedby, and expose dynamic errors accessibly when they are added or removed.

items: Give each input a visible label and an appropriate name.
Mark required fields and explain non-obvious constraints in visible text.
Do not communicate errors through color alone.
After validation fails, identify the field and say how to fix it, for example: “Enter an email address in the format name@example.com.”
Test using Tab, Shift+Tab, Space, arrow keys for radio groups, and Enter to submit.

blocks.prompt: Which attribute supplies the key used for an input's value in submitted form data?

options.feedback: The name attribute supplies the control's key in submitted form data.
The id identifies an element in the document and can associate it with a label.
Placeholder provides a hint inside a control; it does not identify the submitted value.
Autocomplete helps the browser recognize or fill a value, but it is not the submitted field key.

blocks.explanation: Keep the document identifier (id), submitted-data key (name), hint (placeholder), and autofill hint (autocomplete) separate.

blocks.prompt: Adding type="password" to an input encrypts its value before the browser sends the form.

options.feedback: Password inputs visually mask characters; the input type does not encrypt the value.
The input type changes presentation and semantics, not transport encryption. Use HTTPS and appropriate server-side security.

blocks.explanation: Visual masking, transport encryption, and server-side credential handling solve different problems.

blocks.prompt: Which practices improve a form's semantics and usability? Select all that apply.

options.text: Associate a visible label with each control
options.feedback: An associated label communicates the control's purpose.

options.text: Use placeholder as the only description of a field
options.feedback: Placeholder disappears during typing and is not a reliable replacement for a label.

options.text: Group related radio choices with fieldset and legend
options.feedback: Fieldset and legend establish a semantic group and its shared question.

options.text: Rely on browser validation instead of server checks
options.feedback: Client-side checks help usability but are not the sole validation or security boundary.

blocks.explanation: Good form UX combines semantic labels and groups with validation on both client and server boundaries.

blocks.title: Build an accessible registration form
blocks.context: Create a registration form for a fictional learning platform. Focus on labels, native browser behavior, and semantic grouping. No backend is needed; the action URL is illustrative.
instructions: Create fields for full name, email, and password.
Give each field a visible label, a unique id, and a meaningful name.
Choose appropriate input types and autocomplete values; mark required fields.
Add a fieldset/legend group for a preferred contact method with two radio choices.
Add a terms checkbox with a visible associated label.
Add a submit button with an explicit type.
Open the page and test each control using only the keyboard.
requirements: The form has action and an explicit method; if there is no backend, the endpoint is clearly illustrative.
Every control has an accessible name.
Radio options share one name but have different values and ids.
Labels are associated with controls and are not replaced by placeholders.
Native validation blocks empty required values and checks email format.
Keyboard focus is visible and controls can be operated without a mouse.
blocks.starterCode: Create an account
hints: Decide each control's id, name, type, and visible label before styling it.
Mutually exclusive radio options share a name and have different values.
Press Tab from the start of the page to verify a logical focus order.
successCriteria: The document has a complete HTML shell and a semantic main region.
Every control has an explicit label association and a submitted-data name.
required and email fields trigger native validation when invalid.
Radio options are semantically grouped and behave as one choice.
The form can be understood and operated using a keyboard.
You can explain what the browser validates and what the server must validate.

items: Form defines the submission destination and method; controls collect values.
Label and id associate the visible label with the control; name is the key in submitted data.
Placeholder is a hint, not a label. Native constraints improve usability but do not secure a server.
Use fieldset/legend for related controls and explicit button types for predictable behavior.
Accessibility includes accessible names, group context, keyboard operation, visible focus, and understandable errors.
